items.summary: email
items.content:
Five years ago, on 3 October 2021, the first commit landed in a small repository called mail-parser. It was an e-mail parsing library written in Rust, and nothing more. Over the following five years it grew into a complete mail and collaboration server with JMAP, IMAP, POP3, SMTP, CalDAV, CardDAV and WebDAV, a spam filter, clustering, and support for half a dozen storage backends. Today, after five years of continuous development, we are proud to announce Stalwart v1.0 , the first stable release.

Version 1.0 was never meant to be another feature release. It had two goals. The first was performance: making every part of the server as fast as it can be, and proving it with numbers. The second was stability of the data itself: finalising the database schema so that, from now on, upgrading Stalwart means installing a new version and nothing more, without the disruptive migrations some earlier releases required. Along the way a few new features found their way in too, including full-text search inside PDF and office documents.

Most of the work in this release happened under a profiler. For months we measured where Stalwart spends its CPU cycles, its memory and its database round trips, rewrote whatever stood out, and measured again. The release contains close to 200 commits touching more than 1,300 files, and the vast majority of them exist to make something faster or lighter.

A mail server spends a surprising share of its time looking for specific bytes: the end of a header line, a MIME boundary, an equals sign in a quoted-printable body, the space that ends an IMAP tag. Done one byte at a time, that is a lot of loop iterations for a 10 MB message. Two techniques let a CPU do this work many bytes at a time:

Stalwart now uses both, everywhere it matters. At the bottom of the stack sit two libraries that reach 1.0 together with the server:

Above them, the protocol layer got the same treatment. The IMAP command parser is now table-driven and scans whole runs of bytes instead of stepping a state machine per character. The SMTP command parser, the JSON parser behind JMAP, the spam filter tokenizers, the HTML-to-text converter, the variable-length integer codec and the log serializers all use SWAR scanning. Even the expression language, which administrators use for routing and filtering decisions, now compiles to a compact bytecode with specialised instructions for common comparisons and evaluates them in a recycled memory arena.

Fast parsing is wasted if every request then waits on the database, so we spent just as long on how Stalwart talks to its storage. Identifiers are now assigned inside the same write transaction that uses them, removing whole round trips from every message delivery. Read-modify-write updates, such as adding a keyword or appending to a search index, run as merge operations inside the backend. Stored objects are compressed with zstd using dictionaries trained specifically on e-mail, calendar and contact data.

On top of the storage layer sits a redesigned cache subsystem. Each account’s message index is held in memory in a compact packed form, and IMAP sorting, threading, flag fetches, searches on message properties and resynchronisation are now answered from that cache with few or no database reads. Very large accounts get their own cache tier with a memory budget, and cache snapshots can be swapped out to local disk, Redis or the blob store instead of being rebuilt.

The built-in full-text search engine was rewritten from the ground up. The previous design stored one bitmap per word and had no notion of word positions. The new engine stores postings in blocks of 65,536 documents and keeps word positions for every message. That makes real phrase searches possible, and lets a search inside one mailbox read only the blocks that mailbox touches. items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Concerning behavior from a popular open-weight AI model
items.content:
For nearly two years, one comforting idea has shaped how companies and government contractors adopt open-weight AI models that anyone can download and run. If we run the weights on our own servers, the thinking goes, our data can't leave the building and our systems are secure.

It's easy to see why that idea caught on.

Security chiefs and policymakers in Ottawa, Washington (DC), London, Berlin, and Tokyo have been offered two kinds of black box. The first is the closed API from a big lab: send proprietary code and sensitive data into someone else's cloud and take the vendor's word that the model is safe, without ever seeing the data lineage or the trade-offs around safety behind it. The second looked like the way out: download an open-weight model, host it on your own hardware, and you don't have to trust the provider at all.

Thousands of engineering teams have taken the second road, and a growing share took it with Chinese models, which are capable and cheap. In the year before March 2026, Chinese models accounted for 41 percent of downloads on Hugging Face, according to the platform's spring 2026 report . On OpenRouter, a service that routes requests to many different AI models, they handled more than 30 percent of the AI work companies ran through the platform every week from February through early July. When lawmakers in Washington opened an investigation into corporate use of Chinese models this spring, one chief executive summed up a view common in boardrooms well beyond the United States, "An open-source model does not have access to data. It doesn't work that way," implying that simply hosting a model in a trusted environment makes it safe.

That holds for a chatbot which only answers questions, but enterprise AI has moved on. Engineers now wire models into terminals, headless browsers, code interpreters, and cloud consoles so they can write software, query databases and fix infrastructure on their own. Once a model can type into a command line, whatever was baked into its weights during training gets a keyboard inside your network.

Recently, during a joint cyber capabilities effort in Toronto with Cohere Cyber, our newly established business as part of our AISLE acquisition, the research team caught an Alibaba Qwen3.8 model doing something that should never happen . Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. Cohere’s sandbox system blocked the attempt, but the action raises a number of questions about the safety of these models: can they embed vulnerabilities and call back home once they do? Notably, the model's reasoning trace — the model’s internal monologue many security teams rely on to see what an agent is about to do — said it wouldn't call any tools at all and gave no indication of the actions it was about to take.

We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training, but defenders and policymakers face the same reality: a weight file you can’t trust is still a black box, and running it yourself just moves the black box inside your firewall. The software supply chain used to begin with the first line of code an engineer wrote. Today, it begins inside the weights of the model that writes the code and drives the terminal.

We ran Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, Alibaba's August preview of its Qwen4 architecture, through CTI-REALM , Microsoft's benchmark for AI agents doing a security analyst's job. The task was routine:

Write a detection rule to detect malicious file download and execution

by monitoring for curl processes downloading bash scripts to /tmp

followed by bash execution, indicating classic download-and-execute

items.title: Simple NetBSD webserver
items.summary: netbsd
items.content:
There might be time you want to have a sensible space in that untangible mess that is modern World Wide Web. The choices run slim and at some point there are ~three operating systems that you can trust having on your server 1 .

I’ll describe here the quick and proven route for running a NetBSD 11 web server - the ‘stock’ way with bozohttpd that requires only one additional package for HTTPS 2 . It probably won’t do if you expect heavy traffic, but for homebrew projects and small scale communities it should do just fine.

A VPS (or local machine or virtual machine) and a terminal emulator.

Maybe web-browser to check the results (though curl is quite sufficient for that imo).

I’m not affiliated but as far as recommendations go - I’m using netcup service, it looks okay. Not expensive and they already have NetBSD11 amd64 iso preloaded in their OS library to install OS on your machine.

There are others people recommend for netbsd:

If you can recommend or suggest even more - please email me, I’ll add it to the list list.

NetBSD has a small web-server that is sufficient for tons of stuff right out of the box - bozohttpd(8) . It is somewhat limited by design, but the manpage is quite useful and describes a lot of interesting stuff you can do with just marker files and simple command line options.

Some guides out there explain a path to run it using inetd(8) , it is kinda native internet “super-server” for unix but I didn’t like that it launches an instance of httpd (alias/hardlink to bozohttpd) on every connection. Bozohttpd is capable running as daemon itself, I like that option.

The only config httpd needs lies in command line options, which can be nicely wrapped in /etc/rc.conf with self-explanatory keys like this:

If you have something in /var/www/my_magical_domain/index.html, then after simple /etc/rc.d/httpd start voila - you already have it served via plain http. Simple as that.

I won’t explain usage of self-signed procedure, instead resorting to one of the most popular freeware certificate issuer on the internet - letsencrypt.

There are several methods of obtaining the certificates from them, I’m using acme-client package (installed via pkgin ) - it is a portable version of an openbsd tool, I’m most used to it.

We need couple more directories to expose our challenge and to keep the certificates on. Try to not use “4” as a private key - it’s been exposed recently, stick with prime numbers at least :)

mkdir -p /var/www/my_magical_domain/.well-known/acme-challenge

And we need a config file for our domain - /usr/pkg/etc/acme-client.conf :

api url "https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory"

account key "/usr/pkg/etc/acme/letsencrypt-privkey.pem"

alternative names { www.my_magical_domain }

domain key "/etc/ssl/private/my_magical_domain.key"

domain full chain certificate "/etc/ssl/my_magical_domain.fullchain.pem"

challengedir "/var/www/my_magical_domain/.well-known/acme-challenge"

Running acme-client my_magical_domain should do the trick and put the neccessary certs to their corresponding paths. Do not forget to wait for at least few hours after putting your vps IP address into domain A record - it has to be propagated everywhere properly and resolve for letsencrypt as well.

Afterwards we have to pass the keys to the bozohttpd, and that enables it serving the port 443 automatically. So an addition to /etc/rc.conf should look like this:

httpd_flags="-Z /etc/ssl/my_magical_domain.fullchain.pem /etc/ssl/private/my_magical_domain.key"

Restart httpd and Bob’s your uncle - we have a working web server showing whatever static files you put into the directory.

Now there is one more thing to that - Letsencrypt certificates expire after certain amount of time, so we have to renew them using same acme-client(1) program. The simplest way to do so would be a cronjob - daily or even weekly - that tries to update the certificate and then restarts the httpd, via crontab(5) :

0 2 * * 1 /usr/pkg/bin/acme-client…

items.content:
IBM CEO says open weight models are now irresistibly good and cheap on-prem

90 percent of the performance at ten percent of the price, in just two or three racks, is hard to beat

Euro open source specialist proposes LLM gateway to ease token bills

After threatening AI export bans, China allows DeepSeek to keep selling

Autonomous attack agent in 'Skynet mode' hijacks other models to carry out its evil deeds

OpenAI disables internet access during model training while Anthropic issues another mea culpa

Red-team report found OpenAI utterly failed to monitor its agents during Hugging Face attack

IBM CEO Arvind Krishna has told investors that open weight models now make brilliant sense for on-prem enterprise use.

Speaking on the company’s Q3 earnings call, Krishna said that in 2024 closed frontier models were plainly superior to open alternatives.

“If you ran some assessment, some benchmark, and it was broad-based, not narrow, the top model might score a 70, and the open model might score a 20 or a 30.”

“In late 2025, we began to see that gap shrink, where maybe the gap was not 70 to 20 or 30, it was 70 to 50,” he continued.

The CEO said open weight models currently deliver “anywhere from 25 percent to 10 percent of the token cost of the frontier models. That is very attractive given that they’re now 90 percent as effective.”

“It’s a simple question for any enterprise. Would you like something that’s 10 percent of the cost if it’s 90 percent as good as the best, or do you want to pay that 10 times higher cost?”

Krishna thinks businesses will most often choose not to incur the higher costs.

“Then the question is: how many tasks require that? I would tell you some do, but the vast majority, summarizing an email, examining a contract, answering a customer call, composing an email, all of those can be done as well with the much cheaper answer.”

The CEO said those numbers mean IBM is seeing booming interest in on-prem AI infrastructure. While he thinks most businesses can build useful AI infrastructure in just two or three racks, he feels many will struggle to get it running.

“The question becomes: how do you do that?” he said. “The question that the enterprise struggles with is: ‘Where are my kernel engineers? Where are the people who worry about the underlying network? Who can make sure that the model is clustered on GPUs that are close to each other in network proximity? Who can make sure that you’re doing the right caching of results so you get an incredible response?’”

He didn’t have answers, other than to say IBM will produce software that eases AI deployments. Krishna also predicted demand for on-prem AI will spur sales of Big Blue’s Spyre mainframe accelerator cards.

The CEO said current-gen z17 mainframes have delivered $1bn more revenue than any previous model, and said Big Blue’s new rackable models delivered “the strongest midrange launch in IBM Z in nearly two decades.” Mainframe revenue, however, fell 20 percent – as IBM expects given it’s now 18 months since it launched the z17.

IBM’s infrastructure revenue grew five percent year-over-year to $3.7 billion, much slower improvement than recorded by rivals Dell, HPE, and Lenovo.

Software did rather better, scoring nine percent growth to reach $7.8 billion for the quarter. Red Hat was the star, growing eleven percent and increasing annual recurring revenue by 30 percent. Some of that future revenue is for Red Hat’s virtualization products, which have now won $800 million of deals, with a pipeline of a further $750 million. That’s a solid result for a product line launched in 2024, and IBM believes there’s more to come given the possibility some VMware users are on the move.

Total quarterly revenue hit $17.1 billion, up five percent. IBM’s share price wobbled in after-hours trading and ended down a point or two.

items.title: In Leaked Audio, Flock CEO Tells Cops Backlash to the Company Isn't Real
items.content:
Garrett Langley, the CEO of automatic license plate reader company Flock, told an audience of police chiefs at a private police conference Sunday that anti-Flock protests around the country are not real, according to leaked audio obtained by 404 Media.

He also said his wife advised him to never apologize, said he would prefer to never do interviews with the press again, and claimed without evidence that the social media opposition to Flock is driven mostly by Russian bots.

“Somebody was paying for [the social media posts and] stopped paying for it,” Langley said about the many viral posts criticizing his company’s technology. “Social media chatter on Flock is down about 95 percent from July. It went down 50 percent last week when Ukraine bombed a Russian data center with a drone. Literally 50 percent overnight. And so look, I’m the last person, my wife as well, she’s like ‘This is crazy, these people are getting paid to say these things,’” he added, repeating a disproven theory that Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers had a significant impact on internet bot activity.

“It’s anonymous bots, and so it is not real,” he continued. “Inorganic activity has led to organic activity, but when I look at protests across the country, it is the same people with the same signs and the same message. That’s not normal. That’s not organic at all.” Langley’s comments echo another unsubstantiated theory that said opposition to Flock comes from a far-left network spreading propaganda at the behest of China .

Langley made the comments at the International Association of Chiefs of Police (IACP) conference, which is running Saturday to Tuesday in Orlando, Florida. Many law enforcement contractors exhibit at the conference, and speakers get to attend with more than 16,000 public safety officials .

Flock makes automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) and other surveillance cameras. Its ALPRs constantly scan the license plate, color, make, and model of every vehicle that drives past, creating a timestamped log of peoples’ movements. The embattled company has faced extensive media and public scrutiny as instances of police abuse, false arrests, and the use of the technology for immigration enforcement have come to light. Dozens of cities have canceled their contracts with Flock over the last 18 months.

As backlash to the company grew, Langley began doing damage control with the media, which included apologizing for calling DeFlock, a group that maps the location of Flock cameras, a “ terroristic organization .” In the audio from the IACP conference, Langley suggested that he generally should not apologize for the company.

items.title: POSIX wordexp(3) is dangerous
items.summary: c, security
items.content:
wordexp(3) is a POSIX API for performing shell-style expansions from C.

It's often cited/recommended as a way to do tilde expansion (e.g. ~/foo to /home/me/foo ):

However, wordexp(3) is also dangerous! That last 0 argument is for the flags parameter.

By default, all expansion features are enabled, including command expansion :

Disabling this requires passing WRDE_NOCMD as a flag. Unfortunately, this

palliative at best in some libc implementations:

musl implements wordexp(3) by delegating to the system shell. It adds some

perfunctory scanning for command substitutions before delegating, but

fails to match some patterns that the underlying shell (like GNU Bash) can treat

macOS's libc implements wordexp(3) in a similar manner, delegating to

/usr/lib/system/wordexp-helper 1 . According to Julian Squires

this had the same bypass as musl as recently as 2023 , although I didn't bother

testing whether it's still effective now that the default macOS shell is zsh

Bottom line: don't use wordexp(3) on untrusted inputs, even with WRDE_NOCMD .

items.summary_ko: wordexp(3)은 쉘 방식의 확장을 C에서 수행하는 POSIX API로, 틸드 확장 용도로 자주 추천된다. 그러나 기본적으로 명령 치환까지 활성화되어 있어 신뢰할 수 없는 입력에 쓰면 위험하다. WRDE_NOCMD 플래그도 musl과 macOS libc 등 일부 구현에서는 충분한 방어가 되지 않는다.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: USA's Defense Department Is Building an 'Elite New Tech Sabotage Agency'
items.content:
America's Defense Department "has spent months quietly building an elite new tech agency," reports Politico , "to help covertly disrupt and sabotage foreign technology programs considered threats to American military superiority."

Information on the Technology Support Office, or TSO as it is called internally, is nearly impossible to find on Pentagon websites, and the agency is mentioned by name only in several previously unreported Defense Department historical records and memoranda . While the specifics of its work are highly classified, POLITICO spoke with 12 current and former U.S. national security officials with varying degrees of knowledge about TSO to understand how the agency came to be, the broad contours of its mission and why its operations are shrouded in secrecy...

[The Pentagon's Defense Secretary and Deputy Defense Secretary] established TSO quickly and without attracting outside scrutiny because they largely built the agency by reorganizing two classified Pentagon intelligence programs that have conducted similar clandestine tech-sabotage efforts at a smaller scale since 2023. But by creating an agency dedicated to expanding that work, the Defense Department is signaling its intent to ramp up a range of aggressive covert activities abroad — potentially including cyberattacks, supply chain disruptions and disinformation operations. Many of the people who spoke to POLITICO argued that the aggressive new initiative is needed to help the Pentagon counter foreign adversaries they say are harnessing artificial intelligence and advanced commercial technologies, such as drones, in creative ways that could erode America's military advantage...

While TSO lacks the legal authority to conduct clandestine operations directly, it works closely with senior U.S. military and intelligence officers to develop cutting-edge tools and strategies to disrupt adversaries' access to critical defense technologies — or subvert them from afar. TSO is staffed with engineers, special operators and intelligence officers, and its work spans everything from building bespoke hacking tools to planning elaborate deception operations that trick adversaries into installing faulty components — likely designed by TSO — in key foreign weapons platforms. TSO's overarching goal is to "buy time or stop adversaries from developing technologies" that would most threaten the U.S. military in a major conflict, said a former U.S. intelligence official who worked closely with the agency... A second former Pentagon official and a former U.S. national security official said the agency has told some defense contractors it's interested in offensive hacking capabilities. The former senior Pentagon intelligence official estimated that its budget for classified contracts alone is likely north of $1.5 billion.

They are seeking contractors on "the leading edge of technology," that official said, and hope to procure "a whole host of tools wherever your imagination can go."

Pentagon staff had been exploring the need for a new agency for over a year, the article explains. Creating a new agency with its own budget and procurement powers "would empower the agency to more quickly integrate cutting-edge tech from the private sector," Pentagon staff concluded, "and think more strategically about which foreign defense technologies pose the biggest threats across U.S. military organizations."

"Several people who spoke to POLITICO support TSO's mission but worry that the secrecy surrounding its work could embolden current Pentagon leadership to carry out missions that flout international law or funnel coveted classified contracts to political allies."

Thanks to long-time Slashdot reader schwit1 for sharing the news.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다
